newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek PM Simitis calls for hard work and reform.
newsitem.headline: Greek PM Simitis calls for hard work and reform.

text.p: Socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis and his new cabinet will set to work on Thursday after launching Greece's post-Papandreou era by calling for hard work and reform.
The technocrat premier who won elections on Sunday has made clear he is determined to change the face of Greece to that of a modern European country.
"We will spare no effort so that Greece will really become a country with a different presence and different role," said Simitis, 60, after his cabinet was sworn in on Wednesday.
"The greatest challenges in our area are European unification, a new role in the Balkans, economic development and modernisation," Simitis said.
His call for fast and hard work is a stark contrast to his late mentor Andreas Papandreou, who dominated Greek politics for decades with his flamboyant free-spending policies.
Simitis, a soft-spoken academic who challenged Papandreou in his last years in power, has been frank about the need to deliver bitter medicine to turn the ailing ecomomy around.
"The government aims to operate immediately at a brisk pace...to take advantage of anything positive and fight everything negative," he said.

On Wednesday black-clad Orthodox priests chanted a blessing for the new four-year government. Simitis, followed by 42 ministers and deputy ministers, then swore an oath of office to President Costis Stephanopoulos.
The ceremony marked the end of the Papandreou era, with a new-generation socialist leader and his own hand-picked cabinet setting out a firm pro-Western course.
Simitis succeeded the ailing Papandreou to the premiership in January and took over the party's helm from its legendary founder after his death in June.
Revered by the left, Papandreou was elected Greece's first socialist prime minister in 1981 and won two more landslide victories in 1985 and 1993.

Simitis combined in his cabinet old-guard socialists with young reformers who helped put him in power, delighting markets which took the moderate government as an indication of stability and continuity.

Greek markets also felt reassured by the minimal changes in the economic team. National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou, who cut inflation to single digits for the first time in 20 years, was reappointed and also given the Finance Ministry.
Simitis flexed his muscles by removing defence minister Gerassimos Arsenis. Papandreou's son George, former education minister, got only the number two spot at the Foreign Ministry.
He named as Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos, who has won respect for his skills but raised eyebrows for occasional blunt criticism of some EU partners.
Pangalos's first challenge will be relations with Turkey and a new U.S. effort to lessen tensions between the two NATO states stemming from their disputes over the Aegean and Cyprus.
